name: Fennwick Gloom
equipment: Spellbook (bound in iridescent leather, covered in margin notes and diagrams)
Quarterstaff (arcane focus crystal mounted on top)
A pair of cracked spectacles he refuses to replace (sentimental)
A bottle of ink that changes color based on the writer's mood
A sheaf of papers covered in illusory theory equations
A small mechanical bird (non-magical, winds up and hops)
Robes of many patches (each patch is a different fabric and color)
features: Gnome Cunning (advantage on INT, WIS, and CHA saving throws against magic)
Natural Illusionist (know the Minor Illusion cantrip, INT is the casting ability)
Speak with Small Beasts (can communicate simple ideas with Small or smaller beasts)
Arcane Recovery (recover spell slots equal to half wizard level, rounded up, on short rest — once per day; up to 3 levels of slots)
Illusion Savant (halved time and gold to copy illusion spells into spellbook)
Improved Minor Illusion (Minor Illusion can create both a sound and an image simultaneously)
Malleable Illusions (when casting an illusion spell with duration 1+ minutes, can use action to change the nature of the illusion)
Researcher (Sage feature — when you don't know a piece of lore, you often know where to find it)

personality.traits: I mutter to myself constantly while thinking, often carrying on both sides of a debate simultaneously. I take notes on everything — including conversations, combat, and meals — in increasingly illegible handwriting. I am convinced that Wonderland is a grand illusion spell that became self-sustaining and I intend to prove it.
personality.ideals: Knowledge. Understanding how things work is the highest calling. Wonderland operates on rules that defy conventional magical theory, and if I can crack its code, it could revolutionize our understanding of demiplane construction and illusory magic. The fact that people are suffering here is also important, obviously. Primarily important. But the THEORY—
personality.bonds: My mentor, the great illusionist Abjorra Knibb, spent her life studying the theory of self-sustaining illusions — spells that become real through belief. She theorized that somewhere in the multiverse, such a spell existed. She died before proving it. I carry her final research notes and intend to complete her work. Wonderland may be the proof she was looking for.
personality.flaws: I prioritize understanding over safety with alarming frequency. I will stop mid-combat to take notes on an interesting magical effect. I am also deeply insecure about my own magical abilities — I compensate with illusions because I believe my 'real' magic isn't impressive enough, and Wonderland, where illusion and reality blur, both thrills and terrifies me.

appearance: A small, wiry forest gnome standing 3'4" with wild white hair that stands up in tufts like dandelion fluff, as though perpetually electrified. His skin is the warm brown of walnut wood, and his enormous green eyes — magnified further by cracked spectacles he refuses to replace — give him a look of perpetual startlement. His ears are large and pointed, and they twitch when he's thinking hard (which is always). He wears robes made of dozens of different fabric patches — silk, cotton, burlap, velvet, and materials that defy identification — giving him the appearance of a small, ambulatory quilt. His quarterstaff is topped with a cloudy crystal that occasionally flickers with illusory images of whatever he's thinking about (a side effect of his Improved Minor Illusion that he hasn't figured out how to stop). His hands are perpetually ink-stained, and he usually has a quill tucked behind one ear and a half-eaten sandwich tucked behind the other. He moves in quick, darting motions, like a bird investigating something shiny.
backstory: Fennwick Gloom has been called many things: brilliant, eccentric, scattered, obsessive, and 'a hazard to himself and others' (that last one by three different academy review boards). A prodigiously talented illusionist from a long line of gnomish tinkerers and hedge-wizards, Fennwick showed an early aptitude for illusion magic that bordered on the unsettling — his childhood imaginary friend turned out to be a Semi-Real Phantasm that persisted for six years before anyone noticed it wasn't a real gnome. He studied under the legendary illusionist Abjorra Knibb, who recognized in Fennwick both exceptional talent and exceptional lack of common sense. Abjorra's life's work was the Theory of Autonomous Illusions — the hypothesis that sufficiently complex illusion magic, reinforced by the belief of enough observers, could become permanently real. She called it the 'Wonderland Hypothesis,' named after an old fey legend about a demiplane created from pure imagination. She died before proving it, leaving her notes and her theory to Fennwick. Fennwick has spent the decade since Abjorra's death trying to prove her right. He's created illusions of remarkable complexity and persistence, but none have crossed the threshold into genuine reality. When rumors reached him of a shattered looking glass and a demiplane where illusion and reality were indistinguishable, he nearly tripped over himself in excitement. If Wonderland is what Abjorra theorized — a self-sustaining illusion that became real — then understanding it could reshape magical theory forever. The fact that it's ruled by a tyrannical queen who executes people for painting roses the wrong color is, Fennwick assures everyone, his primary concern. But his notebooks tell a different story: page after page of theoretical equations, magical diagrams, and the same question written in increasingly excited handwriting: 'IS IT REAL? IS ANY OF IT REAL?'
